newsitem.title: UK: Albania hopes to privatise two banks in two years.
newsitem.headline: Albania hopes to privatise two banks in two years.

text.p: Albania hopes to have turned two of its state-owned banks into private hands by 1998, central bank governor Kristaq Luniku said on Thursday.

The selling off of its three banks is one of the measures which Albania has been pressed to implement by the International Monetary Fund, with which it will have fresh talks in November on a new standby programme.
"The process will start immediately...during 1997 and 1998, Rural Commercial Bank and National Commercial Bank will be privatised," he told Reuters in an interview during a visit to London.
Savings Bank is the country's third bank. All three banks should be privatised by 2000.
The key problem facing Albania is to ensure long-term financial stability, he said.
"There are a lot of steps to be taken but we are committed," Luniku said, adding that the country's willingness to privatise the economy had been crucial.
However, he conceded that a new agreement with the IMF would not be easy.
The country's current economic position looked good, with high growth likely to continue.
"Real gdp growth has averaged more than 10 percent in the three years. We expect to have the same in 1996," Luniku said.
Foreign exchange reserves were also up sharply, currently at around $270 million, or 3-1/2 months' worth of imports, while the currency appeared to have stabilised.
The government was intent on continuing to free up prices and Luniku described the recent liberalisation of bread prices as a courageous and successful step.
It would also press ahead with efforts to impose a modern monetary system through both indirect and direct instruments.

During he visit to London, Luniku negotiated the release of $19 million worht of gold, which has lain in Bank of England vaults since 1947 mainly because of a dispute over compensation for two British warships which hit mines off the Albanian coast.
He said the gold would be used for the country's international reserves.
"It's good we reached that agreement. But it is also good that it was not reached with the communist government because who knows where the money would have disappeared to," Luniku added.
